Data from February 2024 showed a significant decrease in visits by container and bulk carrier vessels in January 2024, which marked a two-year low. The Panama Canal is a critical route for the U.S., its largest user, with American commodity exports and imports accounting for about 73% of the canal's traffic. These restrictions and slowdowns particularly impact agricultural exports, including cotton, destined for major Asian markets. <2> The National Cotton Council (NCC) announced the results of its 43rd Annual Early Season Planting Intentions Survey during its 2024 Annual Meeting, projecting U.S. cotton acreage for 2024 to be 9.8 million acres. [1, 4] Consequently, projected ending stocks were reduced by 300,000 bales, bringing the new estimate to 2.5 million bales. [1, 4] Despite these changes in supply, the marketing year average price for upland cotton was projected to remain unchanged at 77.0 cents per pound. [1] <2> An early 2024 report highlighted that an ongoing drought has caused significantly low water levels in the Panama Canal, slowing down U.S. cotton export shipments. A severe lack of rainfall in the region depleted Gatun Lake, which feeds the canal's locks, prompting the Panama Canal Authority (PCA) to restrict the number of daily vessel transits. Data from February 2024 showed a significant decrease in visits by container and bulk carrier vessels in January 2024, which marked a two-year low. Both buyers and sellers acted with caution due to the volatility, while poor downstream demand further impeded sales.
